transcript:
Meeting: Pegasus AI — Latency & Throughput scope
Date: 2026-05-16 17:00 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Alex Rivera (Pegasus CTO), Sana Malik (Pegasus ML Eng), Jon Park (Pegasus Infra)

Summary: Quick discovery focused on p95 latency targets, concurrent request patterns, streaming vs non-streaming, and how Redwood Hosted / Dedicated / Private options affect tail latency and tokens/sec. Customer wants concrete benchmarking steps and a rough capacity/cost estimate for 13B-ish models with quantized weights.

Topics: p95 targets, start-of-stream vs full-sequence latency, batching/caching tradeoffs, KV/prefix cache, sustained tokens/sec, spike/burst handling, security (VPC/KMS/SOC2), next steps for benchmarking.

-- Transcript --
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on the account, and Liam our SE is also here. Quick intros?
[00:12] Alex: Hey, Alex here CTO at Pegasus. We build a real-time summarization layer for financial news, low latency is big for us.
[00:18] Sana: Sana, ML Eng, I run the inference pipeline and the prompt set.
[00:22] Jon: Jon, infra, I care about steady-state throughput and bursting.
[00:28] Liam: Great. Quick call plan — scope out your latency and concurrency SLOs, understand prompt lengths and models, and then we'll propose a benchmark and deployment mode (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private).
[00:41] Alex: Our rough SLO is p95 end-to-end <= 350ms for 1–2k token responses for our summarization requests, and p99 ideally under 700ms. For streaming, we care about first-byte latency < 200ms. Does that sound feasible?
[00:58] Maya: Thanks, that's super helpful. Two clarifying q's — what model family are you planning to run in prod (open model vs closed), and what's expected peak concurrency?
[01:08] Sana: We're experimenting with 13B open models — mainly Llama2-13B and a couple of 13B Falcon variants. Quantized to 4-bit ideally. Peak concurrency: baseline 120 concurrent requests during market open spikes, sustained 40–60 during the day. Bursts up to ~300 for 30–60 seconds.
[01:30] Liam: Okay that helps. For 13B quantized models, p95 sub-350ms is aggressive if you also need 2k token outputs unless you optimize for streaming where first-token latency is the main metric. Two things to separate — first-token/start-of-stream latency, and full sequence completion time which scales with tokens/sec.
[01:51] Jon: We're more concerned with start-of-stream for UX, but we also need predictable total throughput since billing and capacity need to be planned.
[01:58] Maya: Right. For Hosted we typically target predictable first-byte latencies by keeping conservative batching and autoscaling. Dedicated gives you pinning to GPU pools and lower variability, and Private (VPC/on-prem) gives you network isolation but requires more ops.
[02:12] Alex: Curious about kernel & compilation differences — does Redwood auto-select kernels for these quantized weights? We saw mixed results running in-house.
[02:20] Liam: Yes, our runtime does kernel selection and will pick int4-friendly kernels when the model is quantized. There are also sequence-length dependent kernels; the runtime aims to choose the fastest path for your median sequence lengths. The caveat — if your sequence lengths vary a lot, tail latency can increase due to slower path hits.
[02:36] Sana: Can you talk through batching behavior? We worry about batching increasing start latency during spikes.
[02:42] Liam: Absolutely. We do continuous batching with dynamic max-latency knobs. For low-latency configs we essentially run micro-batching — very short batch windows (1–3ms), and coupling that with autoscale so you don't hit large queues. For Dedicated you can also raise concurrency per GPU and tune batch sizes.
[02:59] Alex: So how do you measure tokens/sec for capacity planning? We need an estimate of sustained tokens/sec per GPU for 13B int4 to map to expected throughput.
[03:09] Liam: We use a small harness that runs representative prompts at target sequence lengths. For example, on an A100-class Dedicated instance with 13B int4 we often see X tokens/sec for greedy decoding (I'll give actual numbers after we run your corpus). Important: streaming output amortizes latency differently — you can get lower first-byte latency while throughput depends on tokenization and decode speed.
[03:30] Jon: We also need to understand KV cache reuse — many of our requests share a common prefix (the news event context) so caching could help. Does Redwood support prefix KV cache across requests?
[03:39] Liam: Yes, prefix caching is supported in both Hosted and Dedicated. It can reduce compute per request significantly if your prefixes are reused and cached in GPU memory. We'll want your access patterns to estimate cache hit rate.
[03:48] Sana: There's mention of quantization quality regressions — is there tooling to recommend quantization levels and evals?
[03:55] Maya: Yep — Redwood Optimize provides suggestions and a quick A/B eval harness so you can run quality checks versus your baseline prompts. We tie quality regressions to alerts so you won't accidentally degrade user-facing metrics when switching configs.
[04:08] Alex: Back to numbers — can you give at least a ballpark tokens/sec for 13B int4 on a single GPU so we can do rough math?
[04:16] Liam: Ballpark, and this is workload dependent, but for autoregressive decode on say an A100 equivalent: 13B int4 often yields ~8k–14k tokens/sec for greedy decoding depending on sequence length and kernel path. With sampling/top-k it can be 60–80% of that. For streaming, first-byte latency is often sub-150–250ms on Dedicated with tuned configs.
[04:42] Jon: That helps. So if we assume 10k tokens/sec per GPU and average response 800 tokens, that's ~12.5 responses/sec per GPU, or ~450 responses/min which matches some of our numbers. But how do we handle bursts to 300 concurrent?
[05:00] Liam: For bursts, Dedicated with autoscale and a small warm pool works well — we can keep spare capacity to absorb 2–3x baseline bursts. Hosted also supports burst capacity but is subject to multi-tenant variability; we can set higher burst SLA in enterprise plans. Also consider rate limiting and client-side backpressure to smooth peaks.
[05:16] Alex: Any recommendations on model size tradeoff? We like the 13Bs for cost, but would 7B be a meaningful latency improvement?
[05:23] Liam: 7B models will be faster — often 1.5–2x tokens/sec improvement and lower memory so you can increase concurrency per GPU. But quality might drop depending on your tasks; that's where Redwood Optimize evals help you decide.
[05:36] Sana: For benchmarking, what do you need from us?
[05:39] Maya: A small corpus (50–100 prompts) with distribution of sequence lengths, expected token counts, and a note of which prompts are streaming vs full-output. Also your concurrency distribution (sustained, peak, burst). We run the harness and return a perf matrix: median, p95, p99 for first-byte and completion, tokens/sec, and recommended instance types.
[05:58] Alex: Timeline? We want numbers before next budget cycle — two weeks would be ideal.
[06:02] Maya: That aligns — if you send corpus by 2026-05-20 we can run initial benches and have a results deck by 2026-05-26.
[06:10] Jon: One more infra Q — network egress and VPC peering. If we go Private VPC, do you still manage the serving plane or is it fully customer-managed?
[06:19] Liam: For Redwood Private in VPC mode, control plane can be customer-managed or we provide a customer-controlled control plane depending on agreement. The serving plane can be in your VPC with our operators' access scoped via RBAC and KMS integrations. We'll share the deployment models with tradeoffs.
[06:36] Sana: Security — we need SOC2 and encryption at rest with KMS. Also SSO/SAML for our SREs.
[06:43] Maya: We're SOC2 compliant and we integrate with customer KMS and SAML/SSO. We'll attach the SOC2 summary and our security FAQ in the follow-up.
[06:51] Alex: Pricing question — rough committed capacity vs pay-as-you-go. We like a committed tier if it lowers cost given our predictable daytime load.
[06:58] Maya: We can do Reserved/Dedicated pricing with commit tiers and burst credits. I'll include a pricing snapshot with the benchmark results.
[07:06] Jon: How do you measure and expose token-level cost in the console? We need to map cost to product features.
[07:12] Liam: Console gives token-level breakdown by route/model and per-request traces. You can allocate cost to teams and set alerts on unit-cost regressions.
[07:20] Alex: Anything else that could cause surprises on tail latency?
[07:23] Liam: Yes — garbage collection on the host, unexpected kernel fallbacks, and cache eviction patterns if GPU memory is tight. We instrument those and typically recommend a tuning run where we monitor KV hitrates, batch distributions, and kernel selection histograms.
[07:38] Sana: Can you do an initial run with our spot workload as-is (no prompt rewriting), and then another with recommended prompt / truncation tweaks? We want to see real-world impacts.
[07:46] Maya: Absolutely — we'll run baseline and tuned. That will show you practical gains from truncation/prefix caching and quantization tuning.
[07:54] Alex: Great. Quick recap and owners?
[07:57] Maya: Recap: Pegasus to send prompt corpus + concurrency profile by 2026-05-20 (Alex). Redwood to send lightweight harness + security docs (Maya) and SE to prepare Dedicated perf notes (Liam). Benchmarks and pricing by 2026-05-26.
[08:12] Alex: Sounds good. Thanks, everyone.
[08:16] Jon: Thanks.
[08:18] Liam: We'll follow up with the harness link and some primer notes on how to anonymize prompts if needed.
[08:26] Maya: Thanks all.

Notes: transcript has occasional mis-hearings — e.g., "kernels" transcribed as "carrels" in some auto transcripts; speakers overlapped briefly at 00:41.
